scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The passamezzo originated in 16th-century Italy and was popular through the early 17th century.
It was known throughout Europe, with early printed collections appearing in Germany, Italy, France, and England.
The dance is closely related to the pavane, sometimes considered a faster variant or an elaborated form.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The passamezzo was performed in courtly and social settings during the Renaissance.
It was often part of a suite of dances, serving as a stately opening or main dance followed by livelier triple-time dances.
The dance was associated with elegance and measured grace, reflecting the tastes of Italian and European courts.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The passamezzo is defined by two main chord progressions: passamezzo antico (minor key) and passamezzo moderno (major key).
These progressions form ostinato bass lines repeated throughout the dance.
Listen for the Lute, Keyboard instruments, Ensemble (strings, winds), Occasional vocal accompaniment.
The pulse is 2/2 or 4/4 (binary rhythm).

The passamezzo features a steady, repeating chord progression in minor (antico) or major (moderno) keys, played on lute or keyboard, with a calm and flowing rhythmic feel supporting measured dance steps.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Giacomo Gorzanis composed 24 passamezzi for lute in 1561, including both antico and moderno types paired with saltarelli.
Vincenzo Galilei compiled 24 suites featuring passamezzo, romanesca, and saltarello in 1584.
The passamezzo spread from Italy to Germany, France, and England, where it was adapted and printed in collections.
The passamezzo is a Renaissance Italian folk dance related to the pavane and linked to the development of Baroque dance suites.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Passamezzo is sibling of Pavane: Closely related slow Renaissance dance, often confused or interchanged with passamezzo.
Passamezzo is follows of Saltarello: Triple-time dance typically performed after the passamezzo.
Passamezzo is follows of Galliard: Lively triple-time dance often paired in suites with passamezzo.
Passamezzo is shares music of Romanesca: Related chord progression and bass ostinato pattern.
